p.src: Now Tripitaka sat beneath the lamp in the meditation hall of Baolin Temple, reciting for a while from the Emperor Liang’s Water Repentance and then reading from the Peacock Sutra. He remained there until the third watch before finally wrapping the scriptures and placing them in their case. Just as he was about to rise and go to sleep, there came a sudden clattering outside the door, followed by the hiss and whistle of a violent gust. Afraid that the wind would extinguish the lamp, the elder hurriedly shielded it with the sleeve of his robe. When he saw the flame alternately brighten and dim, fear began to seize his heart. Presently drowsiness overcame him, and he leaned over the scripture table and dozed. Though his eyes were closed and his senses blurred, his mind remained aware. A humming filled his ears as he listened to the sinister wind sighing beyond the window. What a wind it was! Indeed:

p.src: As the elder listened in his hazy dream, the wind swept past; then from outside the meditation hall came a faint cry of “Master!” He suddenly raised his head and looked through his dream. A man stood outside the door, drenched from head to foot, tears streaming from his eyes, ceaselessly calling, “Master.” Tripitaka straightened and said, “Are you some goblin, phantom, uncanny spirit, or evil demon come to make sport of me in the dead of night? I am not one of those given to lust, greed, or anger. I am an upright and honorable monk, charged by the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to journey to the Western Heaven, worship the Buddha, and seek the scriptures. I have three disciples under me, all heroes who subdue dragons and tame tigers, mighty warriors who sweep away monsters and destroy demons. If they see you, they will smash your body, grind your bones, and reduce you to dust. I say this out of great compassion and merciful consideration. Hide yourself and flee far away while there is still time; do not intrude upon my monastic door.” Leaning against the meditation hall, the man said, “Master, I am neither monster nor demon, neither phantom nor evil spirit.” Tripitaka said, “If you are none of those things, why have you come here so late at night?” The man replied, “Master, be so good as to open your eyes and look closely at me.” The elder duly fixed his eyes upon him and looked carefully. p.src: At the sight, Tripitaka turned pale with astonishment. He hurriedly bowed and called out sternly, “Your Majesty, of which dynasty are you the sovereign? Pray be seated.” He hastened to support the man with his hand, but grasped only empty air. He turned back and sat down; when he looked again, the same man was still there. The elder then asked, “Your Majesty, where are you emperor? Over what realm do you rule? Your realm must be in turmoil, with slanderous ministers deceiving and oppressing you, forcing you to flee for your life in the middle of the night. Whatever you have to say, tell me and let me hear it.” Only then did the man, tears dripping down his cheeks and sorrow knotting his brow, recount the past and explain the cause of his plight. He said, “Master, my home lies due west, only some forty li from here. There stands a walled city, the place where my dynasty was founded.” Tripitaka asked, “What is the place called?” The man replied, “I shall not conceal it from you, Master. When I founded my realm, I named it the Kingdom of Black Rooster.” Tripitaka said, “Your Majesty, what calamity has brought you here in such distress?” The man replied, “Master, five years ago my land suffered a drought decreed by Heaven. Not a blade of grass would grow, and the people starved to death. It was a most grievous sight.” Hearing this, Tripitaka nodded and said with a smile, “Your Majesty, the ancients said, ‘When a nation is upright, Heaven’s heart accords with it.’ You must have failed to show compassion for your people. When famine struck, why did you abandon your city and flee? You should open the granaries to relieve the common people, repent your former wrongs and renew your good deeds, and pardon those unjustly condemned by crooked laws. Then Heaven’s heart will naturally return to harmony, and rain and wind will come in their proper seasons.” The man said, “The granaries of my kingdom were empty, and all our money and grain were exhausted. The civil and military officials alike went without their stipends, while even my own meals contained no meat. Emulating King Yu when he tamed the floods, I shared every hardship with my people, bathing and fasting, burning incense and praying day and night. I did this for three years, yet the rivers only ran dry and the wells were drained. Just when all was at its most desperate, a Daoist adept arrived unexpectedly from Mount Zhongnan. He could summon wind and call down rain, and turn stone into gold. He first met my many civil and military officials and afterward came before me. I immediately asked him to mount the altar and pray. His rites truly proved effective: no sooner did his command tablet sound than a torrential rain poured down. I had hoped merely for three feet of rain, which would have been enough, but he said that land parched by long drought could not be moistened so easily and brought down two inches more. Seeing him act with such generosity, I exchanged eight ceremonial bows with him and swore brotherhood, addressing him as my brother.” Tripitaka said, “Your Majesty, that was a cause for boundless rejoicing.” The man asked, “Where was the joy in it?” Tripitaka replied, “Since that Daoist possessed such powers, whenever you needed rain, you could have him make it rain; and whenever you needed gold, you could have him turn things into gold. What could you still have lacked, and why did you leave your royal city to come here?” The man said, “I shared my bed and board with him for only two years. Then spring came again, with crimson apricot and radiant peach trees opening their blossoms and bursting into bloom. Men and women from every household, princes and nobles everywhere, all went out to enjoy the spring scenery. At that time the civil and military officials returned to their offices, while the imperial consorts withdrew to their courts. The Daoist and I walked slowly hand in hand through the imperial garden. When we came unexpectedly to an octagonal glazed well, he cast in some object or other, and ten thousand rays of golden light shone from within. He tricked me into approaching the well to see what treasure lay within. Then, suddenly revealing his murderous intent, he shoved me into the well with a splash, covered its mouth with a stone slab, heaped earth over it, and transplanted a banana tree on top. Alas, I have been dead for three years now—a wronged ghost whose life was taken in a well.”

p.src: When the Tang monk heard that the man was a ghost, he was so terrified that his limbs went limp and every hair stood on end. Having no other recourse, he questioned him again: “Your Majesty, what you say makes no sense at all. If you have been dead for three years, then whenever the civil and military officials and the empresses of the three palaces attended court and saw their sovereign, why did none of them search for you?” The man said, “Master, his abilities are indeed seldom seen in this world. As soon as he had murdered me, he transformed himself there in the garden into my exact likeness, without the slightest difference. He now occupies my throne and has secretly usurped my realm. My two ranks of civil and military officials, my four hundred courtiers, the empresses of the three palaces, and the consorts of the six courts have all become his.” Tripitaka said, “Your Majesty, you are far too meek.” The man asked, “How am I meek?” Tripitaka said, “Your Majesty, that monster indeed has some supernatural power: he assumed your likeness and usurped your realm, while neither officials nor consorts could recognize the deception. But you alone know clearly how you died. Why did you not lodge a charge before King Yama in the underworld and appeal to him for redress of your wrong?” The man replied, “His supernatural powers are immense, and he is on intimate terms with all the officials. The city god often drinks wine with him; all the dragon kings of the seas are his kin; the Equal-to-Heaven of the Eastern Sacred Peak is his close friend; and the ten generations of Yama kings are his sworn brothers. For that reason, there is nowhere I can bring my complaint.”

p.src: Tripitaka said, “Your Majesty, since you had no means to accuse him in the netherworld, why have you come to me here in the world of the living?” The man replied, “Master, how would a poor wronged ghost like me dare approach your door? Before the monastery gate stand the guardian deities, the Six Ding and Six Jia spirits, the Guardians of the Five Quarters, the Merit Officers of the Four Watches, and the eighteen guardian arhats, all following closely beside your horse. Only just now did the Night-Wandering God send me inside on a gust of divine wind. He said that my three years of suffering beneath the water were now complete and told me to come pay my respects to you. He said that among your disciples is a great apprentice, the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, supremely skilled at slaying monsters and subduing demons. I have therefore come to entreat you with all sincerity: please go to my kingdom, seize the fiend, and distinguish falsehood from truth. I shall repay your kindness even if I must knot grass or bear a ring in my beak.” Tripitaka said, “Your Majesty, have you come to ask my disciple to rid you of that monster?” The man replied, “Exactly, exactly.” Tripitaka said, “My disciple is no good at other tasks, but when it comes to subduing demons and catching monsters, nothing suits him better. Yet, Your Majesty, though he may be charged with capturing the fiend, I fear it will be difficult to justify the deed.” The man asked, “Why should it be difficult?” Tripitaka said, “Since the monster possesses such vast powers that he can transform himself into your exact likeness, every civil and military official at court obeys him in word and heart, and every consort and concubine in the three palaces is devoted to him in feeling and affection. However capable my disciple may be, he would never dare resort lightly to arms. If the officials should seize us and accuse us of violating their realm and destroying their kingdom, charging us with high treason and trapping us inside the city, would we not have tried to paint a tiger only to produce a dog?” The man said, “There is still someone on my side at court.”

p.src: Tripitaka said, “Excellent, excellent. It must be a prince of the royal house or some senior attendant who was dispatched to guard a distant region?” The man replied, “No. My principal consort bore me a crown prince, my own son and heir.” Tripitaka said, “Then the crown prince must have been banished by the fiend?” The man replied, “He was not. He remains at the Golden Throne Hall and the Five-Phoenix Tower, sometimes studying the classics with scholars and sometimes attending ceremonies with Daoist adepts. For these three years, however, the crown prince has been forbidden to enter the inner palace and has been unable to see his mother, the queen.” Tripitaka asked, “Why is that?” The man replied, “It is a scheme devised by the monster. He fears that if mother and son should meet, their private talk might reveal the truth and let the secret escape. Thus he keeps them from meeting, so that he may remain there forever.” Tripitaka said, “Your misfortune must have been ordained by Heaven, yet it closely resembles my own. Long ago my father was murdered by a river bandit, and my mother was seized and violated by him; three months later, she gave birth to me. I escaped with my life upon the water and was fortunate to be rescued and raised by my revered master at Gold Mountain Monastery. I remember how I had no parents in my childhood; now the crown prince here has lost both his parents as well. How truly pitiable!”

p.src: Then he asked, “Even if your crown prince is at court, how am I to meet him?” The man replied, “Why should you be unable to meet him?” Tripitaka said, “He is kept under the fiend’s control and cannot even see the mother who bore him. What possible means could a monk like me have of meeting him?” The man said, “He will leave the court tomorrow morning.” Tripitaka asked, “What is he leaving the court to do?” The man replied, “After tomorrow’s morning court, he will lead three thousand horsemen, with hawks and hounds in train, out of the city to hunt. You will certainly be able to meet him. When you meet him, if you will tell him what I have said, he will believe you.” Tripitaka said, “He is but a mortal with ordinary eyes, deceived by the fiend upon the throne. Is there a day when he does not call that creature ‘Royal Father’ several times? How could he be willing to believe my words?” The man replied, “Since you fear he will not believe you, I shall leave you a token.” Tripitaka asked, “What is it?” The man set down the gold-mounted white jade tablet he held and said, “This may serve as the token.” Tripitaka asked, “What is special about this object?” The man replied, “When that Daoist adept transformed himself into my likeness, this treasure alone was missing from his imitation. When he reached the palace, he claimed that the Daoist who had prayed for rain had made off with this tablet. For three years since then, this object has remained missing. If my crown prince sees it, the sight of the object will remind him of its owner, and he will surely avenge this wrong.” Tripitaka said, “Very well. Leave it with me, and I shall have my disciple handle the matter for you. But where will you wait?” The man replied, “I dare not wait. When I leave, I shall again beseech the Night-Wandering God to raise a divine wind and carry me into the inner palace, so that I may send a dream to my principal queen and have mother and son unite in purpose, while you and your disciples act with one heart.” Tripitaka nodded his assent and said, “Then go.”

p.src: The wronged ghost kowtowed and took his leave. As Tripitaka rose to see him off, somehow his foot caught and he tumbled head over heels, startling himself awake. It had all been a dream of Nanke. Flustered, he faced the dim lamp and hurriedly called, “Disciples! Disciples!” Bajie woke and said, “What do you mean by calling ‘Earth God! Earth God!’? Back when I was a bold fellow, I lived solely by eating people and enjoyed rich meat every day. I was truly happy. But you just had to become a monk and make us escort you along the road. You first said we would merely be monks, but now you treat us as servants: by day we carry the baggage and lead the horse, and by night we fetch the chamber pot and tend your feet! Why are you calling your disciples instead of sleeping at this hour?” Tripitaka said, “Disciples, I was just dozing over the table and had a strange dream.” Pilgrim sprang up and said, “Master, dreams arise from one’s thoughts. Before you even climbed the mountain, you were already afraid of monsters. You also worry that the road to Thunderclap Monastery is too long and that you will never reach it, and you yearn for Chang’an, not knowing when you will return. So the more thoughts you have, the more dreams you dream. Old Monkey, by contrast, has a single true resolve: to go west and see the Buddha. Not one little dream ever comes to me.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, this dream of mine was no dream of homesickness. The moment I closed my eyes, a violent wind swept past, and outside the door of my meditation room appeared an emperor, who said that he was the king of the Kingdom of Black Rooster. His whole body was drenched, and tears streamed from his eyes.” Tripitaka then related to Pilgrim, one by one, all that had happened and everything said in the dream. Pilgrim laughed and said, “Say no more. His coming to you in a dream was plainly meant to bring Old Monkey a piece of business. There must be a fiend there who has usurped the throne and plotted to seize the kingdom. I shall go distinguish the true king from the false. Wherever my cudgel falls upon that demon, success will be assured.” Tripitaka said, “Disciple, he said that monster possesses vast supernatural powers.” Pilgrim replied, “Why fear however vast his powers may be? Once he knows Old Monkey has arrived, he will find no way to escape.” Tripitaka said, “I also remember that he left behind a treasure as a token.” Bajie replied, “Master, stop talking nonsense. A dream is only a dream; why persist in taking it for truth?” Sha Monk said, “‘Though you may doubt the uprightness of the upright, you must still beware the benevolence of the unbenevolent.’ Let us light a lamp, open the door, and see what is there.”

Tripitaka said, “Disciple, he said that monster possesses vast supernatural powers.”
Pilgrim replied, “Why fear however vast his powers may be?
Once he knows Old Monkey has arrived, he will find no way to escape.”
Tripitaka said, “I also remember that he left behind a treasure as a token.”
Bajie replied, “Master, stop talking nonsense. A dream is only a dream; why persist in taking it for truth?”
Sha Monk said, “‘Though you may doubt the uprightness of the upright, you must still beware the benevolence of the unbenevolent.’
Let us light a lamp, open the door, and see what is there.”

p.src: Wukong opened the door, and when they all looked, they saw by the light of the stars and moon that a white jade tablet set in gold had indeed been laid beneath the eaves by the steps. Bajie stepped forward, picked it up, and asked, “Brother, what is this?” Wukong said, “This is the treasure a king carries in his hand. It is called a jade tablet. Master, since we have this object, I believe the matter must be true. Tomorrow, leave the capture of the fiend entirely to me. Only, your fortune will have to sink three degrees.” Bajie said, “Fine, fine, fine! It was only a dream, yet you had to tell him about it. Don’t you know how fond he is of playing tricks on people? And now he says your fortune must sink three degrees.” Tripitaka went back inside and asked, “What are those three things?” Wukong replied, “Tomorrow you must take the blame, endure humiliation, and suffer misfortune.” Bajie laughed. “Even one would be hard to bear. How could he endure all three?” The Tang monk was an intelligent elder and asked, “Disciple, what do these three things mean?” Wukong said, “There is no need to explain. Let me first give you two things.”

p.src: The Great Sage plucked out a hair, breathed immortal breath upon it, and cried, “Change!” It changed into a red, gold-lacquered casket. He placed the white jade tablet inside and said, “Master, hold this in your hands. At daybreak, put on your brocade cassock, sit in the main hall reciting scriptures, and wait while I inspect their city. If he truly is a fiend, I will kill him and thereby perform a meritorious deed here; but if he is not, we must avoid bringing disaster upon ourselves.” Tripitaka said, “Quite right, quite right.” Wukong said, “If the crown prince does not leave the city, that will be the end of it. But if, in fulfillment of the dream, he really does come out, I shall certainly lead him here to meet you.” Tripitaka asked, “When he meets me, how should I receive and answer him?” Wukong replied, “When he arrives, I will inform you first. Open the lid of the casket a little, and let me change into a tiny monk two inches tall and enter it. Then hold me inside the casket in your hands. When the crown prince enters the monastery, he will surely bow before the Buddha. No matter how he bows to you, pay him no attention. When he sees that you do not stir, he will certainly order your arrest. Let him take you away. If he beats you, binds you, or kills you, let him do as he pleases.” Tripitaka cried, “Ah! His military law is severe. What if he truly kills me?” Wukong said, “Nothing will happen; I shall be there. If matters reach a critical point, I will naturally protect you. If he questions you, say that you are an imperial envoy from the Eastern Land, a monk journeying to the Western Heaven to worship the Buddha, obtain scriptures, and present a treasure. He will ask, ‘What treasure do you have?’ Then tell him all about the brocade cassock and say, ‘This is only a treasure of the third rank. I also possess fine objects of the first and second ranks.’ When he asks about them, say that the casket contains a treasure that knows five hundred years above, five hundred years below, and five hundred years in between—altogether fifteen hundred years of past and future affairs, all without exception. Then release me. I shall tell the crown prince what was said in the dream. If he believes it, we will go and capture the fiend, first avenging his royal father and second winning honor for ourselves; if he does not believe it, show him the white jade tablet. I only fear that he is too young to recognize it.” Tripitaka was delighted when he heard this. “Disciple, what a marvelous plan! But of these treasures, one is called the brocade cassock and another the white jade tablet; what name will the treasure you transform into be called?” Wukong replied, “Just call it the Throne-Establishing Treasure.” Tripitaka followed his instructions and committed them to memory. Master and disciples could not sleep all night. They longed for dawn so fiercely that they wished they could nod and summon the sun from Fusang, or breathe out and scatter every star across the sky.

p.src: In fact, the Great Sage had deliberately allowed the shot to strike him. Quick-eyed and nimble-handed, he seized the arrowhead, let the feathered shaft trail conspicuously before him, then stretched his legs and ran. Seeing that his arrow had struck the jade rabbit, the crown prince wheeled his horse and galloped ahead of everyone else in pursuit. When the horse ran swiftly, Wukong sped like the wind; when the horse slowed, Wukong went slowly, always keeping just a short distance ahead. Mile after mile he lured the crown prince to the main gate of Baolin Monastery, where Wukong resumed his true form. The rabbit vanished, leaving only an arrow stuck in the threshold. He rushed straight inside and said to the Tang monk, “Master, he is coming! He is coming!” Then he transformed again into a tiny monk two inches tall and crawled inside the red casket.

p.src: Now the crown prince reached the monastery gate. The jade rabbit was nowhere to be seen; there was only a carved-feather arrow lodged in the threshold. The crown prince turned pale with shock and cried, “How strange! How strange! My arrow plainly struck the jade rabbit. How can the rabbit have vanished while only the arrow remains here? It must have lived so many years that it became a spirit.” He pulled out the arrow and looked up. Above the gate were five large characters reading, “Imperially Founded Baolin Monastery.” The crown prince said, “Now I understand. I remember that years ago, in the Golden Throne Hall, my royal father dispatched an official with gold and silks for the monks here to repair their Buddha hall and sacred images. I never expected to come here today. Indeed: Passing a monastery, one pauses to converse with monks, and gains half a day’s leisure in this fleeting life. For now, I shall go inside and look around.”

p.src: The prince leapt down from his horse and was about to enter when the officers and generals escorting him caught up with their three thousand men. Crowding closely around him, they all passed through the monastery gate. The monks of the monastery were thrown into a panic. They all came forward, kowtowed in welcome, and escorted the prince into the main hall to pay reverence to the images of the Buddha. When he raised his eyes after worship and was about to stroll through the galleries to admire the scenery, he suddenly saw a monk seated squarely in the middle. The prince flew into a rage. “What an unmannerly monk! Today half the royal court has accompanied my carriage into the mountain. Though no decree was sent ahead to notify you, so that you could not come out to meet me from afar, now that my troops and horses are at your gate, you ought at least to rise. Why do you remain sitting there without moving?” He ordered, “Seize him!” At the word “seize,” the guards on both sides moved together. They dragged Tripitaka down and hurriedly prepared ropes to bind him. From inside the box, Pilgrim silently recited a spell and commanded, “Heavenly guardians of the Dharma, Six Ding and Six Jia spirits, I am now laying a plan to subdue a demon. This prince knows nothing of it and means to bind my master with ropes. Make haste and protect him. If they truly succeed in binding him, you shall all be held guilty.” Who would dare disobey the Great Sage’s secret command? They held Tripitaka securely under their protection, so that the men could not even touch his bald head. It was as though a wall blocked their way, and they could not draw near his body.

p.src: Hearing this, the prince was furious. “You shameless monk, what nonsense you speak! With your glib and nimble tongue, you boast that your half a garment is splendid and powerful. How is it that my father’s wrong remains unavenged? Tell me, so that I may hear.” Tripitaka took a step forward, joined his palms, and asked, “Your Highness, how many great debts of gratitude does a person born between Heaven and Earth owe?” The prince said, “Four.” Tripitaka asked, “Which four?” The prince replied, “The grace of Heaven and Earth, which cover and sustain us; the grace of the sun and moon, which shine upon us; the grace of the sovereign’s realm and soil; and the grace of our parents, who nurture and raise us.” Tripitaka smiled. “Your Highness’s answer contains an error. A man has only Heaven and Earth to cover and sustain him, the sun and moon to shine upon him, and the sovereign’s realm and soil. How could there be any nurturing grace from parents?” The prince said angrily, “You monks are idle vagabonds who live on others’ food, shave your heads, and defy your sovereign! If a person were not nurtured by his parents, whence would his body come?” Tripitaka said, “Your Highness, this poor monk does not know. But inside this red box is a treasure called the Emperor-Erecting Ware. It knows five hundred years above, five hundred years in the middle, and five hundred years below—fifteen hundred years of past and future events in all. It knows why you have no debt of gratitude for parental nurture, and it has caused this poor monk to wait here for you a very long time.”

p.src: On hearing this, the prince ordered, “Bring it here and let me see.” Tripitaka pulled open the lid of the box. Pilgrim leapt out and darted squeaking to and fro. The prince said, “What could this tiny little man possibly know?” Pilgrim took offense at being called small. He exercised his divine power, stretched his waist, and at once grew to a height of some three feet four or five inches. The soldiers cried out in alarm, “If he grows this quickly, it will take only a few days for him to thrust right through Heaven!” Once Pilgrim had regained his original stature, he stopped growing. Only then did the prince ask, “Emperor-Erecting Ware, this old monk says that you know the good and ill fortune of past and future. Do you use a tortoise shell for divination? Do you cast milfoil stalks? Or do you judge men’s fortune and calamity from passages in books?” Pilgrim said, “I use none of those in the slightest. I rely entirely upon this three-inch tongue, and there is nothing I do not know.” The prince said, “This fellow too is talking nonsense. Since ancient times, the Book of Changes has been profoundly mysterious. It determines all the good and ill fortune beneath Heaven and teaches people what to pursue and what to avoid. Thus the tortoise is used for divination, and milfoil for casting the oracle. What principle supports what you have said? You speak recklessly of calamity and blessing and lead people’s minds astray.”

p.src: Pilgrim said, “Your Highness, do not be impatient. Wait while I explain it to you. You are the crown prince of the king of the Kingdom of Black Rooster. Five years ago, your country suffered a year of drought and famine, and all the people endured misery. Your emperor and his ministers prayed with all their hearts. Just when not a drop of rain would fall, a Daoist came from Mount Zhongnan. He was skilled at summoning wind and calling rain, and could turn stone into gold. Your sovereign was far too fond of petty cleverness and swore brotherhood with him. Did this happen or not?” The prince replied, “It did, it did, it did! Go on.” Pilgrim said, “Then three years ago the Perfected Daoist disappeared. Who is it that has called himself sovereign ever since?” The prince said, “There truly was such a Perfected Daoist. My royal father swore brotherhood with him, and they ate together and slept together. Three years ago, while they were enjoying the scenery in the imperial garden, he raised a divine wind that snatched the gold-mounted white jade tablet from my father’s hand and carried it back to Mount Zhongnan. Even now, my royal father still longs for him. Because he disappeared, my father lost all desire for pleasure, shut the garden tightly, and has kept it closed for three years. Who else could the reigning emperor be but my royal father?”

p.src: Hearing this, Pilgrim could not stop sneering. The prince questioned him again, but he gave no answer and merely continued to sneer. The prince said angrily, “Why does this fellow merely sneer when he ought to speak?” Pilgrim said, “There is much more to tell, but with so many people standing around us, this is no place to speak of it.” Seeing that there was reason behind his words, the prince swept out his robe sleeves and ordered the soldiers to withdraw for the moment. The officers and generals of his escort quickly passed down the order, and all three thousand troops withdrew beyond the gate to encamp. There was now no one else in the hall. The prince sat above, the elder stood before him, and Pilgrim stood to the elder’s left. All the monks of the monastery had also withdrawn. Only then did Pilgrim compose his expression, step forward, and say, “Your Highness, the one carried away by the wind was your own father who begot you; the one now seated on the throne is the Perfected Daoist who came to pray for rain.” The prince said, “Nonsense! Nonsense! Ever since the Perfected Daoist left, the winds and rains have been timely, the kingdom prosperous, and the people at peace. According to you, the man upon the throne is not my royal father at all. I spare you only because I am still young. If my royal father heard such treasonous words, he would have you seized and hacked into ten thousand pieces.” With a fierce rebuke, he drove Pilgrim back. Pilgrim said to the Tang monk, “Well, what did I tell you? I said he would not believe me, and so it is, so it is. Now let us present that treasure to him, exchange our travel permit, and be on our way to the West.” Tripitaka immediately handed the red box to Pilgrim. Pilgrim took it and gave his body a shake, whereupon the box suddenly vanished. It had in fact been transformed from one of his hairs, and he now took it back onto his body. He then raised the white jade tablet in both hands and presented it to the prince.

u.src: Hearing this, Pilgrim could not stop sneering.
The prince questioned him again, but he gave no answer and merely continued to sneer.
The prince said angrily, “Why does this fellow merely sneer when he ought to speak?”
Pilgrim said, “There is much more to tell, but with so many people standing around us, this is no place to speak of it.”
Seeing that there was reason behind his words, the prince swept out his robe sleeves and ordered the soldiers to withdraw for the moment.
The officers and generals of his escort quickly passed down the order, and all three thousand troops withdrew beyond the gate to encamp.
There was now no one else in the hall. The prince sat above, the elder stood before him, and Pilgrim stood to the elder’s left.
All the monks of the monastery had also withdrawn.
Only then did Pilgrim compose his expression, step forward, and say, “Your Highness, the one carried away by the wind was your own father who begot you;
the one now seated on the throne is the Perfected Daoist who came to pray for rain.”
The prince said, “Nonsense! Nonsense!
Ever since the Perfected Daoist left, the winds and rains have been timely, the kingdom prosperous, and the people at peace.
According to you, the man upon the throne is not my royal father at all.
I spare you only because I am still young.
If my royal father heard such treasonous words, he would have you seized and hacked into ten thousand pieces.”
With a fierce rebuke, he drove Pilgrim back.
Pilgrim said to the Tang monk, “Well, what did I tell you?
I said he would not believe me, and so it is, so it is.
Now let us present that treasure to him, exchange our travel permit, and be on our way to the West.”
Tripitaka immediately handed the red box to Pilgrim.
Pilgrim took it and gave his body a shake, whereupon the box suddenly vanished.
It had in fact been transformed from one of his hairs, and he now took it back onto his body.
He then raised the white jade tablet in both hands and presented it to the prince.

p.src: When the Crown Prince saw him, he said, “What a fine monk, what a fine monk! Five years ago you were a Daoist priest who came and tricked my family out of its treasure; now you have disguised yourself as a Buddhist monk and come to present it as an offering.” He cried, “Seize them!” At this single command, the elder was so terrified that he hastily pointed at Pilgrim and said, “You damned Protector of the Horses! You are forever blundering into trouble out of nowhere and dragging me into it!” Pilgrim stepped forward and stopped them all, saying, “Do not make a commotion, or word will get out! I am not called ‘the fellow who established the ruler’; I have a real name of my own.” The Crown Prince said angrily, “Come forward. I shall ask your true name, so that I may send you before the court to be sentenced!” Pilgrim said, “I am that elder’s senior disciple, Sun Wukong, also called Pilgrim. I am journeying with my master to the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures, and last night we came here seeking lodging. My master was reading the scriptures at night, and around the third watch he had a dream. In the dream your royal father told him that the Daoist had treacherously murdered him and pushed him into the octagonal crystal well in the imperial garden, after which the Daoist assumed his appearance. Not one of the civil or military officials at court knows the truth. You were too young to understand anything, so he forbade you to enter the palace and sealed off the garden, most likely for fear that the secret might leak out. Tonight your royal father came especially to ask me to subdue the demon. I feared the man might not be an evil spirit, so I observed him from the air and found that he truly was a monster. Just as I was about to seize him, you unexpectedly rode out of the city to hunt. That jade hare struck by your arrow was none other than Old Sun. Old Sun lured you to the monastery to meet my master and hear the whole sorrowful tale. Every word of it is true. Since you recognize the white jade tablet, why do you not remember the loving care with which you were raised and avenge your own father?”

p.src: When the Crown Prince heard this, grief filled his heart, and he thought sorrowfully to himself, “If I refuse to believe these words, there is nevertheless some truth in them; yet if I believe them, what am I to make of the man I see upon the throne, who is plainly my royal father?” Truly, caught between advance and retreat, his heart questioned his lips; pondering again and again, he restrained his lips while they questioned his heart. Seeing that he remained uncertain, Pilgrim stepped forward again and said, “Your Highness need not doubt. Please return to your kingdom and ask your royal mother how the affection between husband and wife now compares with what it was three years ago. That single question will reveal whether this is true or false.”

p.src: The Crown Prince reconsidered and said, “That is true. Wait here while I go and ask my mother.” He sprang to his feet, tucked away the white jade tablet, and made to leave. Pilgrim caught hold of him and said, “If all your men and horses return with you, word will surely get out; how then can I succeed? You must enter the city alone on a single horse, without attracting attention or making a display. Do not enter through the Zhengyang Gate; you must go in through the rear slaughterhouse gate. When you reach the palace and meet your mother, by no means speak loudly; you must talk quietly and in a low voice. That monster possesses immense magic powers. If the news should suddenly reach him, neither you nor your mother would escape with your lives.” The Crown Prince respectfully obeyed his instructions. Leaving the monastery gate, he instructed his officers, “Remain encamped here and do not move. I have a matter to attend to. Wait until I return, and then we shall enter the city together.” Just look at him:
